title: Consumer Product Case: From Opportunity to Outcome
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Consumer Product Case: From Opportunity to Outcome. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start with the progress people are trying to make: obtain the right groceries within a budget and time window while trusting that important household needs will be respected. “Reduce abandonment” is an organisational outcome. It becomes useful only when connected to the customer situation producing it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at frame the opportunity around progress?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Combine behavioural evidence with context. Funnel data can show when people leave; interviews, observation, support contacts, search queries, and fulfilment records can explain the conditions around that behaviour. Segment by meaningful circumstances—not just demographics.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A parent managing allergies, a shopper on a strict budget, and someone planning a recipe may interpret the same substitute very differently.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Write an opportunity statement that keeps the need and constraint visible: “People need to understand and control substitutions before purchase because an unsuitable replacement can waste money, break a meal plan, or create a health risk.” This gives the team a richer target than conversion.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at map the whole experience?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Trace the journey from planning and search through selection, checkout, picking, delivery, review, and recovery. Add the backstage service: inventory freshness, fulfilment policy, picker tools, incentives, support authority, refund rules, and data returned to the catalogue.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: At each stage ask:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: What does the person believe is happening? What information do they need before making a commitment? What does the organisation know, and how reliable is it? Who makes the next decision? What happens when reality differs from the expected path?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This exposes causal distance. A checkout complaint may originate in inventory latency; a confusing picker choice may originate in weak catalogue relationships; a refund spike may originate in a policy that prioritises basket completion over suitability.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Generate alternatives at different system levels
turns.text: What changes when we look at generate alternatives at different system levels?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not move directly from insight to interface. Explore changes to information, interaction, policy, operations, incentives, and recovery.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Possibilities include showing inventory confidence earlier, letting customers define substitution rules by category, allowing “contact me” only for consequential items, giving pickers better equivalence information, or automatically refunding unsuitable substitutions without a support negotiation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Compare concepts against customer value, operational feasibility, accessibility, privacy, business outcome, and failure consequence. A detailed preference system may offer control but create setup burden. A universal “no substitutions” choice may protect trust but reduce order completion.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The best direction may combine lightweight defaults with targeted control where consequences are higher.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build the consumer target system?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team models objects and states:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: item, variant, ingredient/allergen claim, price and promotion; inventory observation with source and age; basket intent and substitution preference; proposed substitute, price difference, and equivalence reason; picker decision and unavailable state; customer approval where reachable; charge adjustment, delivery, rejection, refund, and correction.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It defines authority by consequence. A same-brand size change within a customer-set price rule may be permitted. An allergen-sensitive, infant, medical, religious, or explicitly “no substitute” item cannot be replaced merely because a recommendation is similar. “Contact me” needs an expiry and fallback so a picker is not blocked indefinitely.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The intervention combines:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. earlier inventory confidence and substitution expectation in search and basket; 2. lightweight rules by item/category with one-off override; 3. clear substitute comparison—quantity, unit price, ingredients, key differences, and reason; 4. a picker tool that exposes customer constraints and safe alternatives; 5.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: stateful notification with limited decision window and accessible channel; 6. automatic price protection and low-friction refund/rejection; 7. feedback that corrects preference/catalogue relationships without treating every acceptance as universal truth.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This is not “a brighter checkout.” It changes information, interaction, fulfilment, incentives, data, and recovery together.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at prototype the riskiest decisions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose fidelity based on uncertainty. Test wording and information order with sketches. Test the end-to-end decision with a clickable prototype containing unavailable items, price differences, allergies, and time pressure. Test backstage feasibility with fulfilment staff using realistic inventory cases. A polished happy path would conceal the very behaviour that matters.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Observe whether people understand the promise, can predict what will happen, notice consequential differences, recover from a mistake, and retain control. Include keyboard and assistive-technology use. Ask participants to explain the rule in their own words rather than relying on preference statements.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at define outcome and guardrails?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a balanced measurement model. The primary outcome might be successful orders people consider acceptable. Supporting measures can include substitution acceptance, repeat purchase, preference use, refund resolution, and time to complete.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Guardrails should cover unsuitable replacements, allergy-related incidents, price surprises, inaccessible completion, picker workload, support volume, and unequal outcomes across meaningful segments.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Launch in stages, monitor qualitative and operational signals, and define who can pause the change. A conversion lift does not justify a design that increases harmful substitutions or silently transfers more work to customers and staff.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team distinguishes:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: outcome: completed orders that customers judge usable and acceptable after delivery; diagnostics: inventory accuracy, preference coverage, response window, picker decision time, substitute reason, price adjustment, and refund path; guardrails: unsafe/allergen substitution, consent violation, price surprise, inaccessible decision, picker overload, support burden, lower fulfilment for budget-constrained shoppers, and repeated wrong substitute; countermetrics: checkout conversion beside post-delivery acceptance, refund, trust, and repeat willing purchase.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The initial rollout excludes consequential categories until ingredient and restriction data can support them. It includes representative low-stock regions, slower connections, assistive technology, and time-pressured fulfilment. A pause owner can disable automatic substitution while leaving explicit customer approval available.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at produce a defensible consumer case?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The learner’s case should show:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: opportunity and present workaround; behavioural pattern plus contextual mechanism; service journey and backstage incentives; object/state and authority model; alternatives and trade-offs; prototype of normal, unavailable, consequential, interrupted, and recovery states; accessibility and privacy decisions; measures, guardrails, rollout, and ownership; evidence limits and next decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Conversion frame: cart completion replaces acceptable household outcome. Preference overload: people must configure every item before receiving value. Silent delegation: accepting substitutions once becomes permission for unrelated future choices. Catalogue certainty: volatile inventory or incomplete ingredient data appears authoritative.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Picker externality: customer control creates unmeasured decision time and pressure backstage. High-frequency coercion: repeated prompts exploit time pressure or notification fatigue. Refund as safety: money is returned but health, time, meal, or trust harm remains. Easy-market pilot: affluent, well-stocked regions make service quality appear universal.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior product design is the ability to find the real leverage point without losing sight of the person’s outcome. The screen is often where a system decision becomes visible—not where it was created.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Consumer scale magnifies small defaults. Senior practitioners connect growth metrics to fulfilment truth, represent people who cannot absorb a wrong purchase, and understand how ranking, inventory, incentives, and repeated consent reshape behaviour. They remove friction selectively without removing informed choice.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a meal-delivery product. A team begins with abandoned repeat orders, investigates whether timing, choice, price, or unreliable delivery is responsible, tests several interventions, and measures completed meals and complaint patterns.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The case connects opportunity, research, interaction, service delivery, and outcome instead of presenting a polished screen as the solution.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This case uses the complete course: experience framing, research, journey mapping, information architecture, content, interaction, accessibility, service design, prototyping, analytics, and rollout. lesson 202 applies the same reasoning to expert enterprise work, where density, roles, and auditability change the design response.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a consumer journey and trace one visible friction backward through information, policy, data, incentives, and operations. Propose three interventions at different system levels. For each, name the evidence needed, the customer outcome, one externalised burden, and one guardrail that could stop rollout.
